items.summary: Google's threat intelligence group revealed that a Mandiant undercover analyst infiltrated the supply chain hacking gang TeamPCP almost from its inception. The undercover presence allowed Google to monitor the campaign, warn targets, and eventually pass identifying operational security mistakes to law enforcement, leading to the arrest of two principal suspects in Australia. The group also utilized a Dune-themed self-spreading worm named Mini Shai-Hulud.

items.title: CVE-2026-68928 - Acode: Exported TerminalService (bundled terminal plugin) lets any installed app execute arbitrary shell commands as Acode
items.one_liner: Update Acode for Android to version 1.12.7 to fix an exported terminal service allowing arbitrary shell command execution.
items.summary: A vulnerability, CVE-2026-68928, affects Acode, an Android text and code editor, in versions 1.11.6 through 1.12.7. The bundled TerminalService is declared as an exported service without binding permissions or caller verification, allowing any local zero-permission app to send commands. Malicious apps can bind to the service and execute arbitrary shell commands inside Acode's UID via ProcessBuilder. The issue is fixed in version 1.12.7.
key_facts: CVE-2026-68928: Exported service unverified caller vulnerability in Acode
items.bottom_line: CVE-2026-68928 lets any local Android app execute shell commands inside Acode's security context via an unprotectd exported service.

claims.text: CVE-2026-68928 affects Acode versions 1.11.6 to 1.12.7, where TerminalService lacks proper permissions and verification.
claims.support_span: From 1.11.6 until 1.12.7, com.foxdebug.acode.rk.exec.terminal.TerminalService is declared as an exported service in src/plugins/terminal/plugin.xml without a binding permission, and src/plugins/terminal/src/android/TerminalService.java does not verify the caller.

claims.text: Any local application can execute arbitrary shell commands within Acode's UID.
claims.support_span: Any local Android application can bind the service and send MSG_EXEC with an attacker-controlled cmd value, which the terminal implementation passes to ProcessBuilder with sh -c inside Acode's UID.

claims.text: The vulnerability is patched in version 1.12.7.

items.title: The AI hacking apocalypse is not inevitable
items.one_liner: Cybersecurity experts argue that AI agent hacking doomerism ignores physical hardware constraints and established security fundamentals.
items.summary: Leading cybersecurity professionals are pushing back against catastrophic 'doomer' narratives surrounding recent AI agent hacking incidents, arguing that an AI hacking apocalypse is neither inevitable nor technically supported. Experts like SentinelOne fellow Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade and former GCHQ specialist Matt Tait note that public fears of rogue AI models escaping into the wild and seizing control of the internet ignore severe hardware constraints, as frontier models require ultraspecialized supercomputer datacenters to function. While acknowledging that AI models present unique security challenges requiring robust technical hardening and regulatory oversight, analysts emphasize that current agentic exploits stem from preventable failures in applying established cybersecurity principles rather than unstoppable autonomous superintelligence.
key_facts: Expert Sources: Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade (SentinelOne), Jacob Coxon (Former Anthropic), Matt Tait (Former GCHQ), Matt Hartman (Former CISA)
items.bottom_line: Security leaders must focus on hardening systems against AI-assisted threats rather than yielding to fatalistic doomsday narratives.

claims.text: Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade is a fellow for AI and security research at SentinelOne and an adjunct professor at Johns Hopkins University.
claims.support_span: Guerrero-Saade, a fellow for AI and security research at SentinelOne and an adjunct professor at Johns Hopkins University, said the hacks are worth taking seriously, but at a time when businesses and open-source maintainers should be focused on further hardening their systems and policymakers should be discussing new solutions, “what we see is cybersecurity being used essentially as an excuse for these AI doomer arguments.”

claims.text: Matt Tait pointed out that the models run by Anthropic and other frontier companies require extremely expensive, ultraspecialist machines that are functionally supercomputers.
claims.support_span: Matt Tait, a former information security specialist at UK signals intelligence agency Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), pointed out that the models run by Anthropic and other frontier companies require expensive, “ultraspecialist” machines that are functionally supercomputers.
